facts.statement: The first fossils of Ctenurella were discovered in the Strunde valley within the Paffrather Kalkmulde.
facts.quote: The first fossils were found in the Strunde valley in the Paffrather Kalkmulde.

facts.statement: Ctenurella had reduced armor consisting of only a few thin plates on its head and shoulder region.
facts.quote: As with other ptyctodonts, the armor of Ctenurella was reduced to a few thin plates on the head and shoulder region.

facts.statement: Ctenurella was relatively small for a placoderm, reaching a length of just 13 cm.
facts.quote: It was also relatively small for a placoderm, at just 13 cm in length.

facts.statement: Ctenurella possessed two dorsal fins and a rear body section that was relatively long and low.
facts.quote: Ctenurella had two dorsal fins and the rear of the body was relatively long and low.

facts.statement: While most ptyctodonts likely fed on the ocean floor, Ctenurella's well-developed fins suggest it probably also swam in open waters.
facts.quote: Most ptyctodonts are presumed to have fed on the ocean floor, but the well-developed fins of this genus indicate that it probably also swam in open waters.

facts.statement: Male Ctenurella possessed hook-shaped sex organs known as claspers.
facts.quote: Males also had hook-shaped sex organs, known as claspers.

facts.statement: Researchers think that the analogous features found in unrelated living chimaeras and ptyctodonts like Ctenurella represent an example of convergent evolution.
facts.quote: Since analogous features are also found in the unrelated living chimaeras, chimaeras and ptyctodonts are thought to be an example of convergent evolution.

facts.statement: In 1997, Long split the species Ctenurella gardineri into the new genus Austroptyctodus, restricting the genus Ctenurella to sites in Germany.
facts.quote: The species Ctenurella gardineri was split off into the new genus Austroptyctodus by Long (1997) in his review of the Gogo ptyctodontid species, stipulating that the genus Ctenurella as only coming from the German sites.

facts.statement: A 1997 description by Long revealed that the original restoration of Ctenurella gladbachensis incorrectly showed the skull-roof bones meeting behind the nuchal plate.
facts.quote: A new description of Ctenurella gladbachensis by Long (1997) showed that the original restoration had wrongly restored the skull-roof as the central bones do not in fact meet each other behind the nuchal plate.

facts.statement: Ctenurella lived during the Givetian to Frasnian stages, between 383.4 and 379 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Givetian to Frasnian (383.4 to 379 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ctenurella belongs to the family Ptyctodontidae.
Ctenurella is classified within the class Placodermi.
